answer_text:
Let

\[
f^n(x)=\frac{P_n(x)}{Q_n(x)}
\]

be written in lowest terms, so \(\gcd(P_n,Q_n)=1\). We will determine \(\deg Q_n\), which is the minimal possible denominator degree.

For \(n=1\),

\[
f^1(x)=x-\frac1x=\frac{x^2-1}{x},
\]

so

\[
P_1(x)=x^2-1,\qquad Q_1(x)=x,
\]

and hence

\[
\deg P_1=2,\qquad \deg Q_1=1.
\]

Now suppose

\[
f^n(x)=\frac{P_n(x)}{Q_n(x)}
\]

is in lowest terms. Then

\[
f^{n+1}(x)
=f\!\left(f^n(x)\right)
=\frac{P_n}{Q_n}-\frac{Q_n}{P_n}
=\frac{P_n^2-Q_n^2}{P_nQ_n}.
\]

We need to check that this fraction is already in lowest terms. Since \(\gcd(P_n,Q_n)=1\),

\[
\gcd(P_n^2-Q_n^2,P_n)=\gcd(Q_n^2,P_n)=1,
\]

and similarly

\[
\gcd(P_n^2-Q_n^2,Q_n)=\gcd(P_n^2,Q_n)=1.
\]

Therefore

\[
\gcd(P_n^2-Q_n^2,\;P_nQ_n)=1.
\]

Thus we may take

\[
P_{n+1}=P_n^2-Q_n^2,\qquad Q_{n+1}=P_nQ_n.
\]

Now let

\[
a_n=\deg P_n,\qquad b_n=\deg Q_n.
\]

Since \(a_1=2\) and \(b_1=1\), we have \(a_n>b_n\). Hence

\[
a_{n+1}=\deg(P_n^2-Q_n^2)=2a_n,
\]

and

\[
b_{n+1}=\deg(P_nQ_n)=a_n+b_n.
\]

From \(a_{n+1}=2a_n\) with \(a_1=2\), we get

\[
a_n=2^n.
\]

Then

\[
b_{n+1}=2^n+b_n,\qquad b_1=1.
\]

So

\[
b_n=1+2+4+\cdots+2^{n-1}=2^n-1.
\]

Thus the denominator in lowest terms has degree

\[
\deg Q_n=2^n-1.
\]

Finally, if \(f^n(x)=p(x)/q(x)\) is any polynomial representation, then reducing to lowest terms shows that \(Q_n(x)\) must divide \(q(x)\). Therefore every such \(q\) has degree at least \(\deg Q_n\). Hence the minimal possible denominator degree is exactly

\[
d_n=2^n-1.
\]

\[
\boxed{2^n-1}
\]

27B·v4.method: Induction on reduced form f^n=P_n/Q_n; recurrence Q_{n+1}=P_n·Q_n with no cancellation; solve degree recurrence b_{n+1}=a_n+b_n, a_n=2^n to get b_n=2^n−1.
